newGuide.title: Earn college credit in high school without wasting courses
newGuide.description: Compare dual enrollment, ASU Universal Learner and Sophia. Plan around high-school approval, age rules, funding and the college degree you want.
newGuide.lede: You can make progress toward college before high school ends. The useful head start is a course your future degree can use, at a price your family understands. Start with one good choice, then build from there.

sections.heading: 1. Decide what you want the course to count toward
paragraphs: A course can help with a high-school requirement, a future college degree, or both. Those are separate decisions. Your high school or homeschool program determines the high-school side; the college awarding your future degree decides which college requirements it accepts.

Choose a likely school and degree if you have one. If you are exploring, save a few course options and compare their fit across supported degree plans before buying. For example, an introductory business course that becomes an elective at one college might fill a named requirement at another. The course title alone cannot tell you that.

sections.heading: 2. Check the local dual-enrollment option first
paragraphs: A local college partnership may cost less than a course you buy yourself. Ask your school counselor for the participating colleges, available subjects, enrollment dates and approval process. Include homeschool or private-school arrangements when those apply to you.

Florida provides one specific example. Its dual-enrollment program includes eligible students in grades 6–12 and home education. College readiness and articulation requirements apply, with separate home-education provisions. State law exempts eligible dual-enrollment students from registration, tuition and laboratory fees and addresses free instructional materials. That does not make every independently purchased online course part of the funded program.

Use the rules for your own state and school. Check transportation, scheduling and any remaining expenses alongside tuition. A genuinely useful course with funded tuition can be a better first choice than a paid subscription.

sections.heading: 3. Know which kind of academic record you will earn
paragraphs: University coursework and ACE-recommended courses offer different routes. Both can be useful, but neither guarantees a place in every degree. Keep the original provider, course code and completion date in your course collection.

Save the original course identifier and completion date as well as the title. A completed row in your collection is not yet a degree award. Keep the receiving college’s decision alongside that row when it arrives. If you change majors, reuse the original record to compare alternatives instead of retaking it without checking.

sections.heading: 4. Follow the student and parent enrollment steps
paragraphs: ASU has a registration route for high-school learners and additional parental-consent steps for those under 18. Its identity rules permit a birth certificate to begin a course for an under-18 learner, but a proctored exam requires government-issued identification. Check the selected course before assuming the same documents work for every assessment.

ASU currently charges $25 to enroll and an optional $400 to add eligible completed coursework to its transcript. The credit-purchase choice lasts one year after completion; official transcript ordering can add a separate charge. High-school credit is still determined separately. For Sophia, use the provider’s current enrollment and identity instructions rather than assuming ASU’s consent process applies there too.

sections.heading: 5. Keep college application status on your checklist
paragraphs: College credit earned during high school does not automatically make you a transfer applicant. ASU expressly treats learners taking college courses while still in high school as first-year applicants. It defines transfer applicants using at least 12 transferable credits completed after high school.

Other colleges set their own application categories and scholarship rules. Record when you will graduate and when each college course will be completed. Check the target school’s first-year rules before taking additional courses after graduation, particularly if you want the traditional campus experience. This is an admission decision, separate from how much credit the school applies.

sections.heading: 6. Make a small plan you can actually finish
paragraphs: Start with one course that fits your preparation, school schedule and likely degree. Leave room for assignments, grading and transcript delivery. Flexible enrollment does not mean every course can produce a transcript immediately.

Your first checklist can be short: choose the requirement, confirm the high-school arrangement when needed, compare the full cost, complete any consent and identity steps, and save the original record. Mark a course complete only after you finish it; record the receiving college’s award separately. Add the next course when this process feels manageable.

callout.text: Know the course, the requirement it is meant to fill, who issues the academic record and which costs your family will actually cover.

refreshedMilitaryGuide.title: Military college credit: start with JST, CCAF, and the right questions
refreshedMilitaryGuide.description: A practical guide for service members and veterans to collect military education records, request evaluation, compare exams, and check program-specific funding.
refreshedMilitaryGuide.lede: Military learning can be an important part of a degree plan. Begin with your actual education records and the receiving school’s evaluation, then combine useful awards with any college courses, exams, or certifications you already have.

sections.heading: Find the record that documents your learning
paragraphs: The Joint Services Transcript records specified military learning and ACE recommendations. Current VA guidance directs Army, Navy, Marine Corps and Coast Guard learners to JST, and Air Force or Space Force learners to Parchment. Follow the original-record instructions for your history, including any separate civilian college transcripts.

Air University has changed its transcript procedures as CCAF records were integrated into its student information system. Older instructions can conflict with the current process. Begin at the official registrar page and follow the route it provides for your record and access. Keep civilian college transcripts and exam reports on your collection list too.

sections.heading: Request an evaluation for a particular degree
paragraphs: The VA explains that schools decide how many military credits they will accept. There is no universal number of college credits for a military occupation, rank, or length of service. Two schools, or two degrees at one school, may apply the same learning differently.

Send the required official record and ask for the resulting placements. Useful questions are where the learning applies, whether it is lower- or upper-level, and whether any award overlaps another item. Keep the original record in your inventory even when one degree has no room for part of it; another suitable target may use it differently.

sections.heading: Combine records without counting the same learning twice
paragraphs: A learner may have military training, civilian courses, professional certificates, and credit examinations covering related topics. List each original source and identify possible overlap before adding up a degree total. A summary transcript or previously accepted award does not remove the need to follow the new school’s documentation rules.

If you have an associate degree or a CCAF-related pathway, ask whether a published articulation applies to your exact award and intended major. A broad partnership can be useful, but it does not establish a complete course map for every program or waive all remaining university requirements.

sections.heading: Consider exams and outside courses only for real gaps
paragraphs: CLEP or DSST can be useful when an exam fills an unmet requirement. DANTES can fund an eligible learner’s first attempt per exam title. College Board also confirms eligible CLEP remote-proctor fees are funded for that first attempt. Eligibility and retakes have separate rules; a veteran or military-family connection does not automatically make every exam free. A funded exam still needs an acceptable score and a receiving-school placement.

Likewise, compare Sophia, Study.com, StraighterLine, institutional courses, and other eligible sources after the military evaluation. A low-cost course that duplicates an award already on your audit is a poor purchase. Ask about current source limits and whether completion before enrollment is required.

sections.heading: Check academic rules and funding separately
paragraphs: An academic policy permitting credit does not establish benefit coverage. Ask the school’s military or veterans office about the exact program, study format, term structure, enrollment load, and benefit you intend to use. Request an individual answer about any military residency exception rather than applying a general civilian model to your situation.

Some accelerated formats have specific funding exclusions. Purdue Global’s current tuition page, for example, states that ExcelTrack programs are not eligible for VA educational benefits or Federal Tuition Assistance. This makes program-level verification important even at a university that otherwise serves military learners. Compare your actual net cost after the relevant offices confirm eligibility.

sections.heading: Compare the military price, including the fees
paragraphs: Military tuition can change which route is cheapest. Match the rate to your affiliation and exact enrollment format before comparing totals. Active duty, veteran, spouse and dependent-child categories are not interchangeable. A tuition discount is also separate from Tuition Assistance or VA benefit eligibility.

Liberty’s published 2026–27 online undergraduate military rate is $250 per credit for qualifying learners after status verification. Its online policy includes eligible veterans and qualifying spouses, excludes residential programs, and lists a separate 15% regular-tuition discount for eligible military children. School-specific eligibility definitions and verification apply.

TESU’s rates effective with the August 2026 term list $250 per credit for eligible non-nursing undergraduate military students, including specified active, Guard, Reserve, spouse, dependent and civilian categories. That is not a blanket veteran rate. Its military Edison Accelerate fee is $3,468 when the applicable TESU-credit threshold is not met: 24 credits for a bachelor’s degree or 12 for an associate degree. Another fee may apply if graduation takes more than 15 months. Books, graduation and outside courses remain separate costs.

Use your confirmed personal tuition quote in DegreeSteps when it differs from the published standard case. Include mandatory fees and the remaining university work. Keep a pending scholarship or benefit separate until approved, and do not add discounts together unless the school explicitly permits that combination.

sections.heading: Choose a workable sequence
paragraphs: Plan around duty, deployment, work, caregiving, technology access, and assessment arrangements. A self-paced course still needs time for preparation and grading. Your university may also have transfer submission or registration deadlines that are separate from a provider’s flexible schedule.

A strong first checklist is simple: collect the right military record, request an exact degree evaluation, then resolve the largest remaining gap. Keep benefit questions and credit questions visible as separate tasks. When the school replies, record the confirmed placements and revise the proposed outside basket before spending more.
